```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
root <- here::here()
headline <- list()   # one-line findings collected as the document runs

tab_file <- function(f) file.path(root, "outputs", "tables", f)
fig_file <- function(folder, f) file.path(root, "outputs", "figures", folder, f)
read_tab <- function(f) if (file.exists(tab_file(f))) readr::read_csv(tab_file(f), show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL

show_tab <- function(f, digits = 3) {
  d <- read_tab(f)
  if (is.null(d)) return(knitr::asis_output(paste0("*Table `", f, "` not found. Run the script that produces it.*")))
  knitr::kable(d, digits = digits)
}
show_fig <- function(folder, f) {
  if (!file.exists(fig_file(folder, f))) return(knitr::asis_output(paste0("*Figure `", f, "` not found. Run the script that produces it.*")))
  knitr::include_graphics(fig_file(folder, f))
}

say <- function(x) cat(x, "\n\n", sep = "")
bullets <- function(x) cat(paste0("- ", x, collapse = "\n"), "\n\n", sep = "")

# Wording rules of thumb used by the automatic interpretations in this document.
# They are conventions, not laws; adjust them if your supervisor prefers others.
strength_r  <- function(r) { a <- abs(r); if (is.na(a)) "unknown" else if (a < 0.1) "negligible" else if (a < 0.3) "weak" else if (a < 0.5) "moderate" else "strong" }
effect_eps  <- function(e) if (e < 0.01) "negligible" else if (e < 0.06) "small" else if (e < 0.14) "moderate" else "large"
effect_v    <- function(v) if (v < 0.1) "negligible" else if (v < 0.3) "small" else if (v < 0.5) "medium" else "large"
sil_words   <- function(s) if (s > 0.5) "strong cluster structure" else if (s >= 0.25) "weak cluster structure" else "no substantial cluster structure"
p_txt       <- function(p) if (is.na(p)) "p = NA" else if (p < 0.001) "p < 0.001" else sprintf("p = %.3f", p)
improve_words <- function(pct) {
  if (pct < 0) "worse than the baseline"
  else if (pct < 5) "no meaningful improvement over the baseline"
  else if (pct < 15) "a modest improvement over the baseline"
  else "a clear improvement over the baseline"
}
r2_words <- function(r2) {
  if (r2 < 0) "negative, meaning the model does worse than simply predicting the average of the evaluation years"
  else if (r2 < 0.1) "very low, so almost none of the variation is explained"
  else if (r2 < 0.3) "modest"
  else if (r2 < 0.5) "moderate"
  else "substantial"
}
set_label <- function(s) c(test = "Test years (2018 to 2019)", stress = "Stress years (2020 to 2022)")[[s]]
```

# Project overview

This report presents the main results of the disease-outbreak project. It summarises the data, statistical tests, prediction models, important factors and district clusters. Tables and figures are loaded from results already produced by the project scripts.

The analysis describes reported outbreak records. It can identify patterns and associations, but it cannot prove that a factor causes an outbreak.

## Project files

The report reads cleaned data from `data/processed/`, modelling data from `data/final/`, and saved tables and figures from `outputs/`. Run the relevant project scripts first if these files are missing.

# Metric guide

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| RMSE / MAE | Prediction error; lower is better. |
| R-squared | Variation explained by the regression model. |
| Precision / Recall | Precision reflects false alarms; recall reflects missed High outbreaks. |
| F1 / ROC-AUC / PR-AUC | Measures classification performance at or across thresholds. |
| Lift | Above 1 indicates a positive association in a rule. |

# The datasets

## What the data files contain

`cleaned_epiclim.csv` holds one row per valid outbreak report after cleaning. `modeling_data.csv` adds the engineered features, the **split** (train, test or stress) and the two targets: `log_cases` for regression and `high_outbreak` for classification.

```{r data-load}
md_path <- file.path(root, "data", "final", "modeling_data.csv")
md <- if (file.exists(md_path)) readr::read_csv(md_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else NULL
if (!is.null(md)) {
  cat("Rows:", nrow(md), "| Columns:", ncol(md), "\n")
  if ("split" %in% names(md)) {
    knitr::kable(count(md, split, high_outbreak) %>%
      tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = high_outbreak, values_from = n, values_fill = 0))
  }
}
```

```{r data-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (is.null(md)) {
  say("*The modelling dataset has not been created yet. Run `06_feature_engineering.R`.*")
} else {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  out <- sprintf("The modelling dataset has **%s** outbreak records and **%d** columns.",
                 format(nrow(md), big.mark = ","), ncol(md))
  if (all(c("split", "high_outbreak") %in% names(md))) {
    sh <- md %>% group_by(split) %>%
      summarise(n = n(), high = sum(high_outbreak == "High"), pct = 100 * mean(high_outbreak == "High"), .groups = "drop")
    out <- c(out, sprintf("**%s:** %s records, of which %d (%.0f%%) are High outbreaks.", sh$split, format(sh$n, big.mark = ","), sh$high, sh$pct))
    te <- sh$high[sh$split == "test"]
    if (length(te) == 1 && te < 100)
      out <- c(out, sprintf("**Caution:** the test set has only %d High outbreaks, so classification metrics are unstable and should be reported with that caveat.", te))
  }
  bullets(out)
}
```

The split is by calendar year, not at random. Models learn from 2009 to 2017, are judged on 2018 to 2019, and are checked once more on the sparse, COVID-era years 2020 to 2022. This mirrors real use, where a model predicts the future from the past.

```{r eda-outcome-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (!is.null(md)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  med <- median(md$Cases); mn <- mean(md$Cases); mx <- max(md$Cases)
  txt <- sprintf("Reported cases have a median of **%s** and a mean of **%s**; the largest record is **%s** cases.",
                 format(round(med), big.mark = ","), format(round(mn), big.mark = ","), format(mx, big.mark = ","))
  if (mn > 2 * med) txt <- paste(txt, "A mean more than twice the median is the signature of a strongly right-skewed outcome, so the log scale is justified.")
  say(txt)
  headline$eda <- sprintf("Outbreak sizes are heavily skewed (median %s, mean %s, maximum %s cases).",
                          format(round(med), big.mark = ","), format(round(mn), big.mark = ","), format(mx, big.mark = ","))
}
```

## Disease burden

```{r tab-disease}
show_tab("eda_disease_summary.csv", digits = 1)
```

  `records` counts outbreak reports, `total_cases` sums reported cases, and `median_cases` shows the typical outbreak size. A disease with many records but a small median produces frequent small outbreaks; one with few records and a large median produces rare large ones.

```{r fig-disease-box, fig.cap="Figure 3: Log cases by disease"}

```

```{r eda-disease-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
  top <- ds[which.max(ds$records), ]
  big <- ds[which.max(ds$median_cases), ]
  say(sprintf("**%s** accounts for %.0f%% of all records (%s). The disease with the largest typical outbreak is **%s** (median %.0f cases).",
              top$Disease, 100 * top$records / sum(ds$records), format(top$records, big.mark = ","), big$Disease, big$median_cases))
}
```

```{r eda-clim-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cm <- read_tab("eda_correlation_matrix.csv")
if (!is.null(cm) && "log_cases" %in% cm$variable) {
```

# Statistical analysis outputs

These tables test whether the patterns seen in the figures are larger than chance. Records from the same district are not independent, so treat p-values as indicative and give more weight to effect sizes.

## Group differences (Kruskal-Wallis)

```{r tab-kw}
show_tab("stats_kruskal.csv", digits = 4)
```

  `H` and `p_value` test whether log cases differ between groups. `epsilon_sq` is the effect size: roughly below 0.01 negligible, around 0.06 moderate, above 0.14 large. A tiny p-value with a tiny effect size means a real but practically unimportant difference.

```{r stats-kw-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
kw <- read_tab("stats_kruskal.csv")
if (!is.null(kw)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  bullets(sprintf("**%s**: H = %.1f, %s, effect size %.3f (%s)", kw$variable, kw$H, sapply(kw$p_value, p_txt), kw$epsilon_sq, sapply(kw$epsilon_sq, effect_eps)))
}
```

## Correlation with outbreak size (Spearman)

```{r tab-sp}
show_tab("stats_spearman.csv", digits = 4)
```

  `rho` ranges from -1 to +1 and measures how consistently two variables rise or fall together without assuming a straight line. `p_holm` is the p-value adjusted for testing many variables at once.

```{r stats-sp-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
sp <- read_tab("stats_spearman.csv")
if (!is.null(sp)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  top <- head(sp[order(-abs(sp$rho)), ], 4)
  bullets(sprintf("**%s**: rho = %.2f (%s), n = %s, adjusted %s", top$variable, top$rho, sapply(top$rho, strength_r), format(top$n, big.mark = ","), sapply(top$p_holm, p_txt)))
}
```

## Association with outbreak class and climate differences

```{r tab-chi}
show_tab("stats_chisq.csv", digits = 4)
```

```{r tab-clim}
show_tab("stats_climate_by_outbreak.csv", digits = 3)
```

  The chi-square table asks whether the share of High outbreaks differs between seasons or zones; `cramers_v` is the effect size. The climate table compares the median of each climate variable in Low and High outbreaks. Disease is excluded from the chi-square test because the High label is defined within each disease, which balances it by design.

```{r stats-chi-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
chi <- read_tab("stats_chisq.csv"); cl <- read_tab("stats_climate_by_outbreak.csv")
out <- character()
if (!is.null(chi)) out <- c(out, sprintf("**%s vs High outbreak**: %s, Cramer's V = %.3f (%s effect)", chi$variable, sapply(chi$p_value, p_txt), chi$cramers_v, sapply(chi$cramers_v, effect_v)))
if (!is.null(cl)) out <- c(out, sprintf("**%s**: median %.2f in Low vs %.2f in High outbreaks (%s)", cl$variable, cl$median_low, cl$median_high, sapply(cl$p_value, p_txt)))
if (length(out) > 0) { say("**Key finding.**"); bullets(out) }
```

## Multicollinearity (VIF)

```{r tab-vif}
show_tab("stats_vif.csv", digits = 2)
```

  A variance inflation factor above 5 to 10 means a predictor is largely explained by the others, which makes linear-model coefficients unstable. Interaction terms usually score high against their own components.

```{r stats-vif-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
vf <- read_tab("stats_vif.csv")
if (!is.null(vf)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  hi <- vf[vf$vif > 5, ]
  if (nrow(hi) > 0) say(sprintf("Variables with VIF above 5: %s. Interpret their linear-regression coefficients with caution.", paste0(hi$variable, " (", round(hi$vif, 1), ")", collapse = ", ")))
  else say("No variable has a VIF above 5, so multicollinearity is not a concern for the linear models.")
}
```

# Regression outputs: predicting outbreak size

The regression models predict `log_cases`. They are always compared with a **baseline** that predicts each disease's typical (median) size. A model is only useful if it clearly beats that baseline.

```{r tab-reg-metrics}
show_tab("regression_metrics.csv", digits = 3)
```

  Each row is a model on one evaluation set. Compare each model's RMSE and R-squared with the `Baseline` row for the same set. `MAE_cases` converts the error back to real cases but is dominated by a few huge outbreaks, so rely on the log-scale columns.

```{r reg-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
rm_ <- read_tab("regression_metrics.csv")
if (!is.null(rm_)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  out <- character()
  for (s in c("test", "stress")) {
    d <- rm_[rm_$set == s, ]
    cand <- d[d$model != "Baseline", ]
    base <- d[d$model == "Baseline", ]
    if (nrow(cand) == 0 || nrow(base) == 0) next
    best <- cand[which.min(cand$RMSE), ]
    pct <- 100 * (base$RMSE - best$RMSE) / base$RMSE
    out <- c(out, sprintf("**%s:** the best model is **%s** with RMSE %.2f against %.2f for the baseline, which is %s (%.1f%% change in error). R-squared is %.2f, which is %s.",
                          set_label(s), best$model, best$RMSE, base$RMSE, improve_words(pct), pct, best$R2, r2_words(best$R2)))
    if (s == "test") headline$reg <- sprintf("On test years the best regression model (%s) shows %s (RMSE %.2f vs %.2f, R-squared %.2f).",
                                              best$model, improve_words(pct), best$RMSE, base$RMSE, best$R2)
  }
  bullets(out)
}
```

## Performance by outbreak history

```{r tab-reg-hist}
show_tab("regression_metrics_by_history.csv", digits = 3)
```

  `has_history = 1` rows belong to a district and disease with an earlier report, so history features carry real information. `has_history = 0` rows only receive a disease-median stand-in, so models should perform much like the baseline there.

```{r reg-hist-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
rh <- read_tab("regression_metrics_by_history.csv")
if (!is.null(rh)) {
  d <- rh[rh$set == "test" & rh$model != "Baseline", ]
  if (nrow(d) > 0) {
    say("**Key finding.**")
    bullets(sprintf("**%s**, %s: RMSE %.2f, R-squared %.2f (n = %s)", d$model,
                    ifelse(d$has_history == 1, "with an earlier report", "no earlier report"), d$RMSE, d$R2, format(d$n, big.mark = ",")))
  }
}
```

## Figures

```{r fig-reg-pred, fig.cap="Figure 10: Predicted against actual log cases, test years"}
show_fig("regression", "01_pred_vs_actual_test.png")
```

  Each dot is one outbreak. Dots hugging the red diagonal are well predicted. A flat horizontal band of dots means the model predicts nearly the same value for everything and has little skill. Dots far above the line are outbreaks the model underestimated.

```{r fig-reg-imp, fig.cap="Figure 12: Random forest permutation importance (regression)"}
show_fig("regression", "03_rf_importance.png")
```

  Figure 12 shows how much prediction error increases when a variable is scrambled: longer bars mean the model relies on that variable more. Figure 13 compares error distributions: lower boxes mean smaller errors, and the baseline box shows what a trivial rule achieves.

## Coefficients and importance

```{r tab-reg-coef}
show_tab("regression_lm_coefficients.csv", digits = 3)
```

```{r reg-coef-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
lc <- read_tab("regression_lm_coefficients.csv"); ri <- read_tab("regression_rf_importance.csv")
if (!is.null(lc)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  pcol <- grep("^Pr", names(lc), value = TRUE)[1]
  tcol <- grep("^t value", names(lc), value = TRUE)[1]
  sig <- lc[lc$term != "(Intercept)" & !is.na(lc[[pcol]]) & lc[[pcol]] < 0.05, ]
  say(sprintf("In the linear model, **%d** terms are statistically significant at the 5%% level (indicative only, because records are not independent).", nrow(sig)))
  if (nrow(sig) > 0) {
    sig <- sig[order(-abs(sig[[tcol]])), ]
    top <- head(sig, 5)
    bullets(sprintf("**%s**: coefficient %.3f (%s)", top$term, top$Estimate, sapply(top[[pcol]], p_txt)))
  }
}
if (!is.null(ri)) say(sprintf("The random forest relies most on: **%s**.", paste(head(ri$variable, 5), collapse = ", ")))
```

  In a linear model on log cases, a coefficient of 0.1 on a variable means one extra unit of it goes with roughly a 10% change in cases, holding the others fixed. Category coefficients are relative to the first (reference) category alphabetically.

# Classification outputs: predicting surges

A report is a **High outbreak** when its cases exceed the 75th percentile of its own disease, calculated on training years.

```{r tab-thr}
show_tab("outbreak_thresholds.csv", digits = 1)
```

  `outbreak_threshold` is the case count above which a report is High for that disease. Small `n_train` values mean the threshold rests on few records and is less reliable.

```{r tab-clf-metrics}
show_tab("classification_metrics.csv", digits = 3)
```

  Compare each model with two baselines. *Always Low* shows how misleading accuracy is. *Previous report rule* predicts High if the last report in that district and disease was above the threshold; a useful model has to beat it. Compare PR-AUC with `prevalence`, the no-skill level.

```{r clf-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cmet <- read_tab("classification_metrics.csv")
if (!is.null(cmet)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  d <- cmet[cmet$set == "test", ]
  cand <- d[d$model %in% c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest"), ]
  rule <- d[d$model == "Previous report rule", ]
  alw <- d[d$model == "Always Low", ]
  if (nrow(cand) > 0) {
    best <- cand[which.max(cand$PR_AUC), ]
    out <- c(sprintf("On the test years, **%.0f%%** of outbreaks are High (the no-skill PR-AUC level).", 100 * best$prevalence),
             sprintf("The best model is **%s**: PR-AUC %.2f (%.1f times the no-skill level), ROC-AUC %.2f.", best$model, best$PR_AUC, best$PR_AUC / best$prevalence, best$ROC_AUC),
             sprintf("At its chosen threshold of %.2f it reaches precision %.2f, recall %.2f and F1 %.2f.", best$threshold, best$precision, best$recall, best$F1))
    cmp <- "No previous-report baseline is available for comparison."
    if (nrow(rule) == 1) {
      gap <- best$PR_AUC - rule$PR_AUC
      cmp <- if (gap < 0.02) sprintf("It does **not meaningfully beat** the simple previous-report rule (PR-AUC %.2f vs %.2f), so the extra modelling adds little.", best$PR_AUC, rule$PR_AUC)
             else sprintf("It beats the simple previous-report rule (PR-AUC %.2f vs %.2f) by %.2f.", best$PR_AUC, rule$PR_AUC, gap)
    }
    out <- c(out, cmp)
    if (nrow(alw) == 1) out <- c(out, sprintf("A model that always predicts Low is right %.0f%% of the time yet catches no High outbreaks, which is why accuracy alone is misleading.", 100 * alw$accuracy))
    bullets(out)
    headline$clf <- sprintf("On test years the best classifier (%s) reaches PR-AUC %.2f against %.2f prevalence; %s", best$model, best$PR_AUC, best$prevalence,
                            if (nrow(rule) == 1 && best$PR_AUC - rule$PR_AUC < 0.02) "it does not meaningfully beat the previous-report rule." else "it improves on the previous-report rule.")
  }
}
```

## Confusion matrix

```{r confusion}
preds <- read_tab("classification_predictions.csv")
d <- if (!is.null(cmet)) cmet[cmet$set == "test" & cmet$model %in% c("Logistic Regression", "Random Forest"), ] else NULL
if (!is.null(d) && nrow(d) > 0 && !is.null(preds)) {
  best_model <- d$model[which.max(d$PR_AUC)]
  thr <- d$threshold[d$model == best_model]
  tp <- preds[preds$set == "test", ]
  cm_tab <- table(Actual = factor(tp$actual, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Low", "High")),
                  Predicted = factor(as.integer(tp[[best_model]] >= thr), levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("Low", "High")))
  cat("Best model:", best_model, "| threshold:", thr, "\n")
  knitr::kable(as.data.frame.matrix(cm_tab))
}
```

  Rows are the truth and columns are the prediction. The bottom-right cell holds correct High predictions, the top-right holds false alarms, and the bottom-left holds High outbreaks the model missed. Precision is the bottom-right cell divided by the right column; recall is the bottom-right cell divided by the bottom row.

## Figures

```{r fig-roc, fig.cap="Figure 14: ROC curves, test years"}
show_fig("classification", "01_roc_test.png")
```

```{r fig-pr, fig.cap="Figure 15: Precision-recall curves, test years"}
show_fig("classification", "02_pr_test.png")
```

  In the ROC curve, a line bowing toward the top-left is better, and the dashed diagonal is guessing. In the precision-recall curve, a line well above the dashed horizontal prevalence line shows real skill. When High outbreaks are a minority, the precision-recall curve is the more honest view.

  Figure 16 ranks variables by how much accuracy drops when they are scrambled. In Figure 17, an odds ratio above 1 raises the odds of a High outbreak and below 1 lowers them. An interval that crosses the dashed line at 1 means the effect is not clearly different from none.

```{r or-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
orr <- read_tab("classification_lr_odds_ratios.csv")
if (!is.null(orr)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  sg <- orr[orr$term != "(Intercept)" & !is.na(orr$p_value) & orr$p_value < 0.05 & is.finite(orr$upper), ]
  if (nrow(sg) == 0) say("No odds ratio is statistically significant at the 5% level.")
  else {
    top <- head(sg[order(-abs(log(sg$odds_ratio))), ], 5)
    effect <- ifelse(top$odds_ratio > 1, sprintf("%.0f%% higher odds of a High outbreak", 100 * (top$odds_ratio - 1)), sprintf("%.0f%% lower odds of a High outbreak", 100 * (1 - top$odds_ratio)))
    bullets(sprintf("**%s**: odds ratio %.2f (95%% interval %.2f to %.2f), meaning %s", top$term, top$odds_ratio, top$lower, top$upper, effect))
    say("Each effect holds the other variables fixed. Category effects are relative to the first (reference) category alphabetically.")
  }
}
```

# Which factors matter most?

Individual variable importances can be hard to compare, so the table below adds them up by **factor group** and normalises each forest to 100%. Permutation importance spreads credit between correlated variables, and grouping reduces that distortion.

```{r factor-groups}
grp <- c(Disease = "Disease type",
         season = "Season and month", month_sin = "Season and month", month_cos = "Season and month",
         zone = "Location", Latitude = "Location", Longitude = "Location",
         Temp_C = "Climate", preci_log = "Climate", LAI = "Climate",
         preci_missing = "Climate", lai_missing = "Climate", temp_missing = "Climate",
         prev_log_cases = "Outbreak history", roll3_log_cases = "Outbreak history",
         log_days_since_prev = "Outbreak history", log_n_prior = "Outbreak history",
         has_history = "Outbreak history")

group_share <- function(imp, col) {
  x <- pmax(imp[[col]], 0)
  data.frame(group = unname(grp[imp$variable]), share = 100 * x / sum(x)) %>%
    group_by(group) %>% summarise(share = sum(share), .groups = "drop")
}

ri <- read_tab("regression_rf_importance.csv")
ci <- read_tab("classification_rf_importance.csv")
if (!is.null(ri) && !is.null(ci)) {
  fg <- full_join(group_share(ri, "pct_inc_mse") %>% rename(reg_share = share),
                  group_share(ci, "mean_decrease_accuracy") %>% rename(clf_share = share), by = "group") %>%
    arrange(desc(reg_share))
  knitr::kable(fg, digits = 1, col.names = c("Factor group", "Regression importance (%)", "Classification importance (%)"))
}
```

```{r fig-groups, fig.cap="Figure 18: Share of random forest importance by factor group", fig.height=4}
if (exists("fg")) {
  fg %>% pivot_longer(c(reg_share, clf_share), names_to = "task", values_to = "share") %>%
    mutate(task = ifelse(task == "reg_share", "Regression", "Classification")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(reorder(group, share), share, fill = task)) +
    geom_col(position = "dodge") + coord_flip() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of importance (%)", fill = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
}
```

```{r factors-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (exists("fg")) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  tr <- fg$group[which.max(fg$reg_share)]; tc <- fg$group[which.max(fg$clf_share)]
  say(sprintf("In the regression forest, **%s** carries %.0f%% of total importance; in the classification forest, **%s** carries %.0f%%.",
              tr, max(fg$reg_share, na.rm = TRUE), tc, max(fg$clf_share, na.rm = TRUE)))
  cl <- fg[fg$group == "Climate", ]
  if (nrow(cl) == 1) say(sprintf("Climate variables together account for **%.0f%%** of regression importance and **%.0f%%** of classification importance.", cl$reg_share, cl$clf_share))
  headline$factors <- sprintf("Most important factor group: %s (regression) and %s (classification); climate contributes %.0f%% and %.0f%%.",
                              tr, tc, if (nrow(cl) == 1) cl$reg_share else NA, if (nrow(cl) == 1) cl$clf_share else NA)
}
```

**Important caution.** These scores describe association, not cause. A variable that ranks high helps the model predict outbreak size; it does not prove that changing that variable would change outbreaks.

# Clustering outputs

K-Means grouped districts by their outbreak profile (reporting frequency, typical size, share of High outbreaks, disease mix, seasonality and climate). Only districts with at least five reports are profiled.

```{r tab-k}
show_tab("clustering_k_selection.csv", digits = 3)
```

  In the elbow plot, look for the point where adding clusters stops reducing the within-cluster spread much. The silhouette measures how well each district fits its own cluster compared with the next closest: above 0.5 is strong structure, 0.25 to 0.5 weak, and below 0.25 essentially none.

```{r clu-say, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cp <- read_tab("clustering_profiles.csv"); ks <- read_tab("clustering_k_selection.csv")
if (!is.null(cp) && !is.null(ks)) {
  say("**Key finding.**")
  k <- nrow(cp); sil <- ks$avg_silhouette[ks$k == k]
  if (length(sil) == 1) {
    say(sprintf("The analysis uses **%d clusters** with an average silhouette of **%.2f**, which indicates **%s**.", k, sil, sil_words(sil)))
    headline$clu <- sprintf("Districts form %d clusters with an average silhouette of %.2f (%s).", k, sil, sil_words(sil))
  }
}
```

## What distinguishes each cluster

```{r tab-clu-prof}
show_tab("clustering_profiles.csv", digits = 2)
```

```{r clu-desc, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
asg <- read_tab("clustering_district_assignments.csv")
if (!is.null(asg)) {
  feat <- intersect(c("log_n_reports", "median_log_cases", "pct_high", "share_monsoon", "share_diarrhoeal", "share_dengue",
                      "share_chik", "share_cholera", "share_malaria", "mean_temp", "mean_preci", "mean_lai"), names(asg))
  zs <- asg %>% mutate(across(all_of(feat), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x)))) %>%
    group_by(cluster) %>% summarise(across(all_of(feat), mean), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
  lines <- character()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(zs))) {
    v <- unlist(zs[i, feat])
    top <- head(names(sort(abs(v), decreasing = TRUE)), 3)
    parts <- sprintf("%s (%+.1f SD)", top, v[top])
    lines <- c(lines, sprintf("**Cluster %s** (%d districts) stands out for: %s.", zs$cluster[i], zs$n[i], paste(parts, collapse = ", ")))
  }
  say("**Cluster profiles.** SD means standard deviations above (+) or below (-) the average district.")
  bullets(lines)
}
```

```{r fig-pca, fig.cap="Figure 21: Clusters in principal-component space"}
show_fig("clustering", "03_pca_clusters.png")
```

```{r fig-prof, fig.cap="Figure 22: Standardised cluster profiles"}
show_fig("clustering", "04_cluster_profiles.png")
```

  Figure 21 flattens the profiles into two dimensions: clusters that overlap heavily are not clearly separated. Figure 22 is a heat map where red or blue cells show which features define each cluster. Figures 23 and 24 show whether clusters are geographic or cut across regions.

```{r scorecard, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
get_h <- function(x) if (is.null(x)) "Not available yet: run the relevant script." else x
sc <- data.frame(
  Objective = c("1. Disease patterns (time, place, seasonality)", "2. Predict outbreak size (regression)",
                "3. Predict surges (classification)", "4. Important factors", "5. District clusters and rules"),
  Headline = c(get_h(headline$eda), get_h(headline$reg), get_h(headline$clf), get_h(headline$factors), get_h(headline$clu)))
print(knitr::kable(sc))
```

# Conclusion

The project describes outbreak patterns by disease, time and location, tests relationships between recorded factors and case counts, and evaluates models for outbreak-size prediction and surge classification. Clustering and association rules add summaries of district and outbreak patterns.

Model usefulness should be judged against the relevant baseline on held-out test years. Results represent associations in the available records, not causal explanations.

## Limitations

This dataset contains reported outbreak events. The analysis therefore focuses on the size and characteristics of recorded outbreaks; it does not directly predict whether a new outbreak will begin. Multiple records can come from the same district, so the usual independence assumptions behind p-values and confidence intervals may not hold fully. Differences in district naming can also split what should be one location into several groups.

Reporting practices may vary across places and years. The 2020–2022 period is especially sparse and unusual, so stress-period results should be treated cautiously. Finally, the patterns identified here are associations. They do not establish that a particular factor causes an outbreak.

## Future work

Future improvements could use regular weekly surveillance data, standardise district names, and test spatial or hierarchical models that account for repeated records from the same districts.
